rewritten_text:
Elizabeth was sad and hopeless. Her usual activities no longer pleased her. Any pleasure seemed disrespectful to the dead, and she believed that endless grief and tears were the only proper tribute to innocence so cruelly destroyed. She was no longer the happy girl who had walked beside the lake with me when we were younger, speaking eagerly of our future. She had suffered the first of those sorrows that loosen our attachment to life, and its shadow had put out her sweetest smiles.

“When I think, my dear cousin,” she said, “of Justine Moritz's terrible death, the world and everything in it look different to me. Before this, the stories of cruelty and injustice I read in books or heard from others seemed to belong to the distant past, or to describe imaginary evils. At least, they were far away: I understood them in my mind without truly picturing them. Now suffering has reached our home, and people seem like monsters hungry for each other's blood. Yet surely I am unfair. Everyone thought the poor girl was guilty. If she had committed the crime for which she died, she would indeed have been among the most wicked people alive. To kill the son of her friend and benefactor for a few jewels—a child she had cared for since birth and seemed to love as her own! I could never agree to anyone's execution, but I would certainly have thought such a person unfit to live among others. Yet she was innocent. I know it; I feel it. You believe it too, and that strengthens my certainty. Oh, Victor, when a lie can look so much like truth, who can feel sure of lasting happiness? I feel as though I am walking along a cliff's edge, with thousands of people pressing toward me, trying to push me into the depths below. William and Justine were murdered, and the killer goes unpunished. He walks freely through the world, perhaps even respected. But even if I were condemned to die on the scaffold for those same crimes, I would never exchange places with that wretched man.”

Listening to her caused me unbearable pain. Though I had not committed the acts myself, I was in effect the real murderer. Elizabeth saw my anguish in my face. She gently took my hand and said, “My dearest friend, you must try to be calm. God knows how deeply these events have hurt me, but I am not as miserable as you are.”

And I don't spring on him straight away and take the chance of bungling the job and only half finishing it. No, I start a long way off to one side and edge toward him by degrees, so he hasn't the least notion that I intend to strike; then suddenly, in a flash, he's lying on his back, unable for the life of him to understand what happened. That was the method I employed upon brother Dowley. I began chatting in an easy, leisurely fashion, as though merely filling an idle hour; and the oldest fellow alive couldn't have plotted my point of departure and guessed where I meant to arrive:

“Boys, there are plenty of peculiar things about laws, habits, customs, and such matters, once you examine them; and about the direction and advancement of human thought and conduct, too. Written laws exist, and they pass away; but unwritten laws exist as well, and those last forever. Consider the unwritten law governing wages. It requires them to rise, bit by bit, throughout the centuries. Observe how the rule operates. We know the present wages in this place and that and another; we average them, and call the result today's wage. We also know what wages were a century ago and two centuries ago. Our information reaches no farther back, but that is enough to establish the rule of progress, the amount and pace of each recurring increase. Thus, with no records to guide us, we can estimate fairly accurately what wages were three, four, or five centuries earlier. Very well. Do we leave it there? Certainly not. We turn from the past and apply our rule to what lies ahead. My friends, name any future date you please, for hundreds upon hundreds of years, and I can tell you what people will be earning.”

“What, good sir, what!”

“Indeed. Seven hundred years hence, wages hereabouts will have climbed to six times their present figure. Farm labourers will receive three cents daily, and mechanics six.”

“Would that I might die this day and live in that one!” broke in Smug the wheelwright, a handsome gleam of greed in his eye.

“Nor is that the whole of it. Their meals will be provided too—such meals as they are; nobody will grow fat on them. Another two hundred and fifty years—listen carefully—and a mechanic's daily wages will be—remember, this follows a law, not a guess—twenty cents!”

An astonished gasp of reverence rose from them all. Dickon the mason lifted his hands and eyes and murmured:

Will you?”

His eyes brightened, and he said:

“I'll help you steal him!”

Well, that knocked all the strength out of me, as if I'd been shot. It was the most surprising thing I'd ever heard, and I have to admit Tom Sawyer sank a good deal in my opinion. Still, I couldn't believe it. Tom Sawyer helping steal an enslaved man!

“Oh, come on!” I said. “You're joking.”

“No, I'm not.”

“Well then,” I said, “whether you're joking or serious, if you hear anything about a runaway slave, remember that you don't know anything about him, and neither do I.”

Then we lifted the trunk into my wagon, and he drove off in his direction while I went in mine. But I was so happy and had so much on my mind that I forgot to drive slowly. I reached home much too soon for the trip I was supposed to have made. The old gentleman stood at the door and said:

“Well, that's amazing! Who'd have guessed that mare could do it? I wish we'd timed her. And she hasn't sweated at all, not one bit. Wonderful! I wouldn't take a hundred dollars for that horse now, I truly wouldn't. Before today I'd have sold her for fifteen and thought that was her full value.”

That was all he said. He was the most innocent, kindhearted old man I'd ever seen. It wasn't surprising, because besides farming he also preached. He had a little plain log church behind the plantation that he'd built himself and paid for himself, to serve as both church and schoolhouse. He never charged for his preaching, and it was worth just what he charged. There were plenty of other farmer-preachers down South who did the same thing.

About half an hour later Tom's wagon stopped at the front stile. Aunt Sally spotted it through the window, only about fifty yards away, and said:

“Why, someone's arrived! I wonder who it is. I do believe it's a stranger. Jimmy”—one of the children—“run and tell Lize to set another plate for dinner.”

Everyone rushed to the front door. A stranger didn't turn up every year, of course, so when one did, he caused more excitement than yellow fever. Tom had climbed over the stile and was walking toward the house. The wagon was hurrying back along the road toward the village, and we were all crowded in the doorway. Tom wore his good, store-bought clothes and had an audience, which always suited Tom Sawyer perfectly.
